atom.definition: The basic particle of elements, consists of protons, neutrons, and electrons
atom.memory-definition: Basic particle of elements, consists of protons, neutrons, and electrons

molecule.definition: A group of atoms held together by chemical bonds
molecule.memory-definition: Group of atoms held together by chemical bonds

isotope.definition: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons
isotope.memory-definition: Atoms of same element with different numbers of neutrons

ion.definition: An atom or molecule with an electric charge
ion.memory-definition: Atom or molecule with an electric charge

valenceShell.definition: The outermost electron shell, denotes valence based on # of electrons
valenceShell.memory-definition: Outermost electron shell, denotes valence based on # of electrons

valence.definition: The number of chemical bonds an atom of a particular element can create
valence.memory-definition: Number of chemical bonds an atom of a particular element can create

bond.definition: Forces of attraction between atoms or molecules
bond.memory-definition: Forces of attraction between atoms or molecules

covalentBond.definition: A force of attraction between two atoms due to them sharing an electron
covalentBond.memory-definition: Force of attraction between two atoms that share electron(s)

ionicBond.definition: A force of attraction between one positively charged ion and one negatively charged ion
ionicBond.memory-definition: Force of attraction between a positively and negatively charged ion

hydrogenBond.definition: A force of attraction between two opposing partial charges involving a hydrogen atom
hydrogenBond.memory-definition: Force of attraction between opposing partial charges involving a hydrogen atom

vanDerWaalsForce.definition: A weak force of attraction resulting from the random movement of electrons
vanDerWaalsForce.memory-definition: Weak force of attraction resulting from random movement of electrons

isomer.definition: Molecules with the same chemical formula but different structures
isomer.memory-definition: Molecules with same chemical formula but different structures

ph.definition: The potential of hydrogen ion dissociation of a substance
ph.memory-definition: Potential of hydrogen ion dissociation of a substance

buffer.definition: Substances which mitigate changes in pH
buffer.memory-definition: Substances which mitigate changes in pH

acid.definition: Substances with a low pH / high rate of dissociation of H+ ions
memory-definition: Substances with high rate of dissociation of H+ ions

base.definition: Substances with a high pH / low rate of dissociation of H+ ions
memory-definition: Substances with low rate of dissociation of H+ ions

electronegativity.definition: The tendency of an atom to attract electrons toward itself
electronegativity.memory-definition: Tendenct of atom to attracts electrons toward itself

polarity.definition: A property of a molecule which has an uneven sharing of electrons
polarity.memory-definition: Property of molecule which has uneven sharing of electrons

cohesion.definition: The sticking together of particles of the same substance
cohesion.memory-definition: Sticking together of particles of same substance

surfaceTension.definition: A result of cohesion which holds together the surfaces of bodies of water
surfaceTension.memory-definition: Result of cohesion which holds together surfaces of bodies of water

adhesion.definition: The sticking together of particles of different substances
adhesion.memory-definition: Sticking together of particles of different susbtances

meniscus.definition: The curved surface of a liquid like water due to adhesion and cohesion in a container.
meniscus.memory-definition: Curved surface of a liquid in a container due to adhesion and cohesion

capillaryAction.definition: The process of a liquid flowing against gravity due to adhesion and cohesion
capillaryAction.memory-definition: Process of liquid flowing against gravity due to adhesion and cohesion

transpiration.definition: The process of water movement through a plant towards its eventual evaporation
transpiration.memory-definition: Process of water movement through a plant toward its evaporation

highSpecificHeat.definition: Water requires much more energy to change temperature than other substances
highSpecificHeat.memory-definition: Water requires more energy to change temperature than other substances

highHeatOfVaporization.definition: Water requires a lot of energy to break the hydrogen bonds and evaporate
highHeatOfVaporization.memory-definition: Water requires lots of energy to break hydrogen bonds and evaporate

solution.definition: A uniform mixture of a solvent and solutes
solution.memory-definition: Uniform mixture of solvent and solutes

solvent.definition: A substance that dissolves another substance

hydrophilic.definition: The property of being attracted to water and/or dissolving in it
memory-definition: Property of being attracted to water

hydrophobic.definition: The property of not being attracted to water and/or not dissolving in it
memory-definition: Property of not being attracted to water
Property of not dissolving in water

essentialElement.definition: The elements that are necessary for life (CHON)
essentialElement.memory-definition: Elements that are necessary for life

macromolecule.definition: A large molecule necessary to life’s biological processes
macromolecule.memory-definition: Large molecule necessary to life's biological processes

hydrocarbonChain.definition: An organic compound containing only hydrogen and carbon arranged in a chain
hydrocarbonChain.memory-definition: Organic compound containing only hydrogen and carbon arranged in a chain

functionalGroup.definition: A group of atoms with distinctive chemical properties separate to that of the total molecule they are attached to
functionalGroup.memory-definition: Group of atoms with chemical properties separate to that of the molecule they are bound to

hydroxylGroup.definition: Polar functional group; hydrogen bound to an oxygen atom

methylGroup.definition: Nonpolar; hydrogen bound to a sulfur atom
methylGroup.memory-definition: Nonpolar functional group; hydrogen bound to sulfur

carbonylGroup.definition: Polar functional group; carbon double bound to oxygen
carbonylGroup.memory-definition: Polar; carbon double bound to oxygen

carboxylGroup.definition: Polar acidic functional group; carbon double bound to an oxygen and a hydroxyl group
carboxylGroup.memory-definition: Polar acidic; carbon double bound to oxygen and a hydroxyl group

aminoGroup.definition: Polar basic functional group; nitrogen bound to 2 hydrogen atoms
aminoGroup.memory-definition: Polar basic; nitrogen bound to 2 hydrogen

phosphateGroup.definition: Polar acidic functional group; phosphate bound to oxygen atoms and hydroxyl groups
phosphateGroup.memory-definition: Polar acidic; phosphate bound to oxygen and hydroxyl groups

sulfhydrylGroup.definition: Polar functional group; sulfur bound to hydrogen atom

monomer.definition: A molecule which can combine with others to form large polymers
monomer.memory-definition: Molecule which can combine with others to form polymers

polymer.definition: A molecule composed of a string of monomers

dehydrationSynthesis.definition: Bonding of two monomer molecules with the removal of a water molecule
dehydrationSynthesis.memory-definition: Bonding of two monomers with the removal of a water molecule

hydrolysis.definition: Splitting of a polymer molecule with the addition of a water molecule
hydrolysis.memory-definition: Splitting of a polymer with the addition of a water molecule

carbohydrate.definition: Macromolecules used by organisms as energy storage and structural materials
carbohydrate.memory-definition: Macromolecules used as energy storage and structural materials

aminoAcid.definition: Monomer unit of a protein; contains carboxyl, amino, and side chain groups

nucleicAcid.definition: Macromolecules used by the organisms to store and express genetic information
nucleicAcid.memory-definition: Macromolecules used to store and express genetic information

lipid.definition: Macromolecules used by organisms to store energy long term, surround cells, and send signals
lipid.memory-definition: Macromolecules used to store energy long term, form membranes, and sned signals

polysaccharide.definition: The polymer made up of monosaccharides; a carbohydrate

structuralIsomer.definition: Molecules with identical chemical formula but differing structural makeup
structuralIsomer.memory-definition: Molecules with same chemical formula but differing structure

enantiomer.definition: Two compounds that are mirror images of each other, but that are not identical
enantiomer.memory-definition: Two compounds that are mirror images of each other, but not identical

alphaAndBetaCarb.definition: Different arrangements of atoms in cyclic forms of sugars that have the same chemical formula
alphaAndBetaCarb.memory-definition: Different arrangements of atoms in forms of sugars that have the same chemical formula

starch.definition: The carbohydrate used by plants for energy storage
starch.memory-definition: Carbohydrate used by plants for energy storage

glycogen.definition: The carbohydrate used by animals for energy storage
glycogen.memory-definition: Carbohydrate used by animals for energy storage

cellulose.definition: A structural carbohydrate which forms plant cell walls
cellulose.memory-definition: Structural carbohydrate which forms plant cell walls

chitin.definition: A structural carbohydrate which forms exoskeletons

triglyceride.definition: The most common lipid, made up of three fatty acid chains and a glycerol molecule
triglyceride.memory-definition: Lipid made up of three fatty acid chains and a glycerol molecule

fattyAcidChain.definition: A linear sequence of carbon atoms with hydrogen atoms attached, ending in a carboxyl group
fattyAcidChain.memory-definition: Linear sequence of carbon with hydrogen atoms attached, ending in a carboxyl group

saturatedFat.definition: A fatty acid hydrocarbon chain without double bonds
saturatedFat.memory-definition: Fatty acid hydrocarbon chain without double bonds

unsaturatedFat.definition: A fatty acid hydrocarbon chain containing double bonds
unsaturatedFat.memory-definition: Fatty acid hydrocarbon chain containing double bonds

steroid.definition: Lipids used for signaling made out of four carbon rings fused together
steroid.memory-definition: Lipids used for signaling made out of four carbon rings

phospholipid.definition: Lipids which contain a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail and make up cell membranes
memory-definition: Lipids which contain a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tail
Lipids which make up cell membranes

cholesterol.definition: The principal steroid; used in animal cell membranes
cholesterol.memory-definition: Principal steroid; using in animal cell membranes

dna.definition: A nucleic acid used to store genetic information
dna.memory-definition: Nucleic acid used to store genetic information

antiparallel.definition: Structure of DNA in which two strands of DNA run alongside each other in opposite directions
antiparallel.memory-definition: Structure of DNA in which two strands run alongside each other in opposite directions

rna.definition: A nucleic acid used to express genetic information
rna.memory-definition: Nucleic acid used to express genetic information

nucleotide.definition: The monomer unit of nucleic acids, contains a pentose, phosphate group, and nitrogenous base
memory-definition: Contains a pentose, phosphate group, and nitrogenous base

nitrogenousBase.definition: Nitrogen containing compounds which are parts of nucleotides (include adenine, guanine, cytosine, uracil, thymine)
nitrogenousBase.memory-definition: Nitrogen containing compounds which are part of nucleotides

adenine.definition: A nitrogenous purine derivative, bound to thymine in DNA base pairing
adenine.memory-definition: Nitrogenous purine derivative, binds to thymine

thymine.definition: A nitrogenous pyrimidine derivative, bound to adenine in DNA base pairing
thymine.memory-definition: Nitrogenous pyrimidine derivative, binds to adenine

guanine.definition: A nitrogenous purine derivative, bound to cytosine in DNA base pairing
guanine.memory-definition: Nitrogenous purine derivative, binds to cytosine

cytosine.definition: A nitrogenous pyrimidine derivative, bound to guanine in DNA base pairing
cytosine.memory-definition: Nitrogenous pyrimidine derivative, binds to guanine

uracil.definition: An RNA specific nitrogenous base which replaces thymine and binds with adenine
uracil.memory-definition: RNA specific nitrogenous base which replaces thymine, binds to adenine

ribose.definition: Five carbon sugar found in RNA backbones
ribose.memory-definition: Five carbon sugar found in RNA backbones

deoxyribose.definition: Five carbon sugar found in DNA backbones
deoxyribose.memory-definition: Five carbon sugar found in DNA backbones

protein.definition: Macromolecules used by organisms for building, repair, and movement
protein.memory-definition: Macromolecules used for building, repair, and movement

peptideBond.definition: Covalent bond between single amino acids

rSideChain.definition: The unique part of each amino acid that differs from the basic amino acid structure
rSideChain.memory-definition: Unique part of each amino acid that differs from the base amino acid

primaryStructure.definition: The linear sequence of amino acids that make up a protein
primaryStructure.memory-definition: Linear sequence of amino acids that make up a protein

secondaryStructure.definition: The structure of the backbone of the polypeptide, excluding side chain interactions
secondaryStructure.memory-definition: Structure of backbone of the polypeptide, excluding side chain interactions

tertiaryStructure.definition: The structure of the polypeptide chain formed from interactions between side chains
tertiaryStructure.memory-definition: Structure of polypeptide chain formed from side chain interactions

quaternaryStructure.definition: The structure of proteins composed of multiple polypeptides
quaternaryStructure.memory-definition: Structure of proteins composed of multiple polypeptides

denaturation.definition: The unfolding or breaking up of a protein due to an environmental change
denaturation.memory-definition: Unfolding or breaking up of a protein due to environmental change

cell.definition: The fundamental biological unit of all living organisms, consisting of a membrane, DNA, a cytoplasm, and ribosomes

prokaryoticCell.definition: Simple cells which contain a single circular strand of DNA, a cytoplasm, ribosomes, and a membrane, but lack compartmentalized organization

eukaryoticCell.definition: A complex cell characterized by the presence of a membrane-bound nucleus, linear chromosomes, and other membrane-bound organelles

cellMembrane.definition: The outer boundary of all cells, separating the cell's interior from its environment, which is semipermeable

cytoplasm.definition: The entire content within a cell's outer membrane, excluding the nucleus in eukaryotic cells

cytosol.definition: The aqueous component of the cytoplasm of a cell

cytoskeleton.definition: A network of protein filaments and microtubules within a eukaryotic cell that provides structural support, maintains cell shape, and facilitates cell movement and intracellular transport

cellWall.definition: A rigid or strong outer layer found in plants, fungi, bacteria, algae, and archaea, but not in animal cells, which provides structural support, protection, and shape to the cell

ribosome.definition: A molecular machine found in all living cells that synthesizes proteins, consisting of a large and small subunit made of rRNA and proteins

organelle.definition: Specialized, membrane-bound structures within eukaryotic cells that perform specific functions necessary for the cell's survival

nucleus.definition: The central part of a eukaryotic cell, containing DNA and controlling cell activities

nuclearEnvelope.definition: The membrane surrounding the nucleus within a eukaryotic cell through which mRNA and ribosomes pass

endomembraneSystem.definition: A network of membranes and organelles within eukaryotic cells that modify, package, and transport lipids and proteins

smoothEndoplasmicReticulum.definition: A network of membrane-bound tubules within eukaryotic cells that lacks ribosomes, giving it a smooth appearance which synthesizes lipids and detoxifies drugs

roughEndoplasmicReticulum.definition: A network of tubules in eukaryotic cells that contains ribosomes and functions in the synthesis and modification of proteins destined for secretion

golgiApparatus.definition: A cellular organelle in eukaryotic cells that functions as a "post office" for modifying, sorting, and packaging proteins and lipids for delivery to their destinations

lysosome.definition: An organelle in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells containing degradative enzymes enclosed in a membrane

vacuole.definition: A space or vesicle within the cytoplasm of a cell, enclosed by a membrane and typically containing fluid

largeCentralVacuole.definition: A significant, fluid-filled organelle in plant cells that serves multiple functions, including storage of water, nutrients, and waste products, and structural support

transportVesicle.definition: Membrane-bound sacs that move molecules, such as proteins and lipids, between organelles within a eukaryotic cell or to the plasma membrane for secretion

secretoryVesicle.definition: A small, membrane-bound sac within a cell that contains materials, such as hormones, enzymes, or neurotransmitters, to be secreted outside the cell

mitochondrion.definition: Organelle responsible for generating most of the chemical energy (ATP) needed to power a cell's biochemical reactions by converting food and oxygen into cellular energy

chloroplast.definition: An organelle in plant and algae cells that carries out photosynthesis, converting light energy into chemical energy in the form of sugars

surfaceArea.definition: The total area of the outer surfaces of a three-dimensional object, measured in square units

volume.definition: The amount of three-dimensional space an object occupies, measured in cubic units

surfaceAreaToVolumeRatio.definition: Calculated by dividing an object’s volume by its surface ratio, with smaller objects having a higher SA:V ratio

membraneFolds.definition: Folds within membranes of cells and cellular organelles, allowing for increased surface area in the same amount of volume

cristae.definition: Folds in the inner membrane of a mitochondrion, the organelle responsible for cellular energy production, that increase surface area to maximize ATP synthesis via cellular respiration

cilia.definition: A short microscopic hairlike vibrating structure found in large numbers on the surface of certain cells, either causing currents in the surrounding fluid or providing propulsion

vesicle.definition: A small fluid-filled bladder, sac, cyst, or vacuole within the body

fluidMosaicModel.definition: Describes the cell membrane as a dynamic structure composed of a lipid bilayer with embedded proteins, carbohydrates, and cholesterol, where components are in constant, fluid motion

bilayer.definition: Structure of all biological membranes, consisting of two layers of phospholipid molecules arranged with their hydrophilic heads facing outward and their hydrophobic tails facing inward

membraneProtein.definition: Specialized proteins that are embedded in or associated with the cell membrane that play roles in cell structure, signaling, and transport

integralMembraneProtein.definition: Proteins embedded into the phospholipid bilayer that have hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions and which pass through the entire membrane (also called transmembrane proteins)

peripheralMembraneProtein.definition: Proteins attached to the surface of the phospholipid bilayer that are not embedded into it and only face one side of the membrane

glycoprotein.definition: A protein with one or more carbohydrate chains, often located on the surface of the phospholipid bilayer, playing a crucial role in cell signaling, recognition, and the immune system

glycolipid.definition: A molecule consisting of a lipid and carbohydrate, located on the surface of the phospholipid bilayer, playing a crucial role in cell signaling, recognition, and the immune system

selectivePermeability.definition: Describes the property of the cell membrane to allow some molecules or ions to pass through while preventing others, maintaining the cell’s internal balance

plasmodesmata.definition: Channels in land plant and algal cell walls that connect the cytoplasm of neighboring cells, allowing for direct transport and communication of molecules like sugars, ions, and proteins

concentrationGradient.definition: Occurs when there is a difference in concentration of a substance between two regions, and the substance will move from areas of high concentration to low until equilibrium is reached

dynamicEquilibrium.definition: The state where opposing biological processes occur at equal rates, resulting in no net change in the system, even though individual components are constantly changing and moving

diffusion.definition: The net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration (following the concentration gradient), driven by the random motion of molecules

passiveTransport.definition: The movement of molecules across a membrane from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration, without the cell expending its own energy

simpleDiffusion.definition: The passive movement of small, uncharged molecules from an area of high to low concentration directly through a cell's membrane, without the use of energy or transport proteins

facilitatedDiffusion.definition: A type of passive transport in which molecules move across a cell membrane through transport proteins (channels or carriers) down their concentration gradient, without additional energy

activeTransport.definition: The cellular process of moving molecules across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, requiring cellular energy, typically in the form of ATP, to drive the process

endocytosis.definition: An active transport process where a cell uses its plasma membrane to engulf and internalize particles, such as large molecules, by forming membrane-bound vesicles

phagocytosis.definition: The process of phagocytes engulfing or ingesting cells to destroy them, a form of active transport

pinocytosis.definition: An active transport process where a cell uses its plasma membrane to engulf and internalize particles liquids and small molecules, by forming membrane-bound vesicles

receptorMediatedEndocytosis.definition: A cellular process where specific molecules bind to cell-surface receptors, triggering the cell to engulf the receptor-ligand complex into a membrane-bound vesicle for internal transport

exocytosis.definition: The biological process where membrane-bound vesicles inside a cell fuse with the cell's outer membrane, releasing their contents to the exterior

channelProtein.definition: Integral membrane proteins that form pores in the membrane, allowing specific molecules or ions to pass through by diffusion

aquaporin.definition: Channel proteins that act as water channels, selectively facilitating the rapid transport of water across cell membranes to maintain water homeostasis and osmotic balance in cells and tissues

carrierProtein.definition: Integral membrane proteins that facilitate the transport of specific molecules, ions, or small particles across the cell membrane by undergoing conformational changes

sodiumPotassiumPump.definition: A protein in the cell membrane that performs active transport, pumping three sodium (Na+) ions out of the cell for every two potassium (K+) ions that are pumped in

membranePotential.definition: The voltage or electrical potential difference across a cell's plasma membrane, generated by the unequal distribution of ions (like sodium, potassium, and chloride) inside and outside the cell

electrochemicalGradient.definition: The combined force driving ions across a cell membrane, resulting from both a chemical gradient (difference in concentration) and an electrical gradient (difference in electrical charge)

osmosis.definition: The net movement of water molecules across a semipermeable membrane from an area of higher water concentration (lower solute) to lower water concentration (higher solute)

tonicity.definition: A solution's ability to influence the movement of water into or out of a cell through osmosis

isotonic.definition: Any external solution with the same solute and water concentrations than the aqueous solutions of cells, resulting in dynamic equilibrium

normalCell.definition: An animal cell in an isotonic solution

flaccidCell.definition: A plant cell in an isotonic solution

hypertonic.definition: Any external solution with a higher solute and lower water concentration than the aqueous solutions of cells, resulting in movement of water outside of the cell

shriveledCell.definition: An animal cell in a hypertonic solution

plasmolyzedCell.definition: A plant cell in a hypertonic solution

hypotonic.definition: Any external solution with a lower solute and higher water concentration than the aqueous solutions of cells, resulting in movement of water into the cell

lysedCell.definition: An animal cell in a hypotonic solution

turgidCell.definition: A plant cell in a hypotonic solution

waterPotential.definition: A measure of the potential energy of water that determines its tendency to move from one area to another, with water always flowing from a region of higher to lower water potential

solutePotential.definition: The effect of dissolved solutes on the water potential of a solution, and water moves from areas of higher solute potential to lower solute potential (opposite of solute concentration)

contractileVacuole.definition: A specialized cellular organelle that functions in osmoregulation by collecting and expelling excess water from the cell to maintain its water balance and prevent bursting

compartmentalization.definition: The organization of a cell or organism into distinct regions or compartments, often by membrane-bound organelles, to allow for specialized functions and efficient processes

anabolicReaction.definition: Reactions which combine small, simple molecules into larger, complex ones, storing energy in the process

catabolicReaction.definition: Reactions which break down large, complex molecules into smaller, simpler ones, releasing energy in the process

endosymbioticTheory.definition: Explains that the first eukaryotic cells formed when a larger host cell engulfed, but did not digest, smaller prokaryotic cells, leading to a mutually beneficial relationship

ancestralEukaryote.definition: A complex, single-celled protist that lived around 2 billion years ago and from which all modern eukaryotes are descended, and that evolved from prokaryotic ancestors through endosymbiosis

mitochondrialDNA.definition: The genetic material found in mitochondria, and is inherited exclusively from the mother, showing proof of the endosymbiotic theory

cyanobacteria.definition: Photosynthetic microscopic organisms that are technically bacteria that evolved to become the modern chloroplast within eukaryotic cells following endosymbiosis

aerobicBacteria.definition: Microorganisms that require oxygen for their growth and metabolism that evolved to become the modern mitochondria within eukaryotic cells following endosymbiosis

enzyme.definition: Proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up specific chemical reactions necessary for life without being consumed in the process

catalyst.definition: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change

activationEnergy.definition: The minimum amount of energy that must be provided to initiate a chemical reaction

activeSite.definition: A region on an enzyme that binds to a protein or other substance during a reaction

substrate.definition: The molecule that an enzyme acts upon

enymeSubstrateComplex.definition: Formed when a substrate molecule binds to an enzyme's active site, allowing a chemical reaction to occur and lowering the activation energy required for the process

lockAndKeyModel.definition: A biochemical concept explaining how enzymes, or biological catalysts, work with high specificity

inducedFitModel.definition: Theory of enzyme-substrate interaction where both the enzyme's active site and the substrate undergo a conformational change upon binding, resulting in a tighter, more precise fit

conformationalChange.definition: Alterations in the three-dimensional shape of a molecule, especially proteins, that are essential for their function, activity, and interaction with other molecules

exergonicReaction.definition: Chemical reactions that break unstable bonds in molecules to release energy; decreases stored energy

exothermicProcess.definition: Reactions that release energy, usually as heat or light, to an organism's surroundings

endergonicReaction.definition: Chemical reactions that create bonds to store energy within molecules; decreases free energy

endothermicProcess.definition: Processes that absorb energy from an organism's surroundings, usually in the form of heat

cofactor.definition: A non-protein chemical compound or metal ion that enzymes need to function as biological catalysts

competitiveInhibitor.definition: Molecules that compete with a substrate for an enzyme's active site, reducing enzyme activity

nonCompetitiveInhibitor.definition: Molecules that reduce an enzyme's activity by binding to a site distinct from the active site, causing a conformational change in the enzyme that hinders its ability to function

allostericSite.definition: A region on an enzyme that is distinct from the active site, where a regulator molecule binds to control the protein's function

feedbackInhibition.definition: A biological control mechanism where the final product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an allosteric enzyme earlier in that same pathway, preventing overproduction

metabolism.definition: All the chemical reactions that occur within a living organism to maintain life, growth, and repair

energy.definition: The fundamental capacity to do work, existing as either potential energy (stored, like chemical) or kinetic energy (in motion, like heat)

atp.definition: A molecule found in all living cells that serves as the primary energy carrier, releasing energy when its bonds are broken

adp.definition: A molecule that is converted from ATP when energy is released for cellular work, with the loss of a phosphate group

energyCoupling.definition: The process where an exergonic reaction (one that releases energy) drives an endergonic reaction (one that requires energy)

1stLawOfThermodynamics.definition: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed from one form to another within an isolated system

2ndLawOfThermodynamics.definition: The entropy of an isolated system tends to increase, meaning biological processes naturally move towards states of greater disorder and energy dispersal

entropy.definition: A measure of the randomness or disorder within a biological system and the dispersal of energy

freeEnergy.definition: The portion of a system's energy that is available to do useful work, such as driving metabolic processes

autotroph.definition: Organisms that produce their own food from inorganic substances in their environment

heterotroph.definition: An organism that cannot produce its own food, instead taking nutrition from other sources of organic carbon, mainly matter from other organisms

stroma.definition: The fluid-filled matrix inside a chloroplast that surrounds the thylakoid membranes, location of light-independent reactions

thylakoid.definition: Membrane-bound compartments within chloroplasts (in plants and algae) and cyanobacteria, serving as the site for the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis

chlorophyll.definition: Green pigments found in cyanobacteria and in the chloroplasts of algae and plants, that allow them to absorb energy from light

stomata.definition: Tiny pores, primarily found on the underside of plant leaves, that regulate gas exchange between the plant and the atmosphere

photosynthesis.definition: The process plants, algae, and some bacteria use to convert light energy, carbon dioxide, and water into chemical energy (glucose/sugars) and oxygen

lightDependentReaction.definition: 1st stage of photosynthesis, occurring in the thylakoid membranes, where light energy is captured by pigments (chlorophyll) and converted into chemical energy (ATP and NADPH)

photosystemII.definition: A large protein complex that initiates photosynthesis by capturing sunlight energy to split water molecules into oxygen, protons, and electrons

electronTransportChain.definition: A series of protein complexes and molecules that transfer electrons, releasing energy used to create an electrochemical gradient that drives ATP synthesis

photosystemI.definition: A multi-subunit protein complex in the thylakoid membrane of plants, algae, and cyanobacteria that uses light energy to facilitate electron transfer, producing NADPH

nadph.definition: A cofactor used to donate electrons for anabolic reactions, including the Calvin Cycle in photosynthesis. NADP+ is the form that accepts electrons, and NADPH donates them.

atpSynthase.definition: A molecular motor in cell membranes that creates ATP, the cell's main energy currency, by using a proton gradient across the membrane

chemiosmosis.definition: The biological process of proton diffusion across a semipermeable membrane down an electrochemical gradient, with the energy from this movement used to synthesize ATP

lightIndependentReaction.definition: 2nd stage of photosynthesis where the energy from ATP and NADPH is used to convert carbon dioxide into organic compounds (glucose) in the stroma

calvinCycle.definition: The cycle where photosynthetic organisms use ATP and NADPH to convert carbon dioxide into glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P), a three-carbon sugar that serves as a precursor for glucose

rubisco.definition: Earth's most abundant enzyme, which play a critical role in carbon fixation (converting inorganic carbon into organic compounds) during the Calvin Cycle

g3p.definition: A three-carbon sugar phosphate formed through the Calvin Cycle; the direct precursor for synthesizing glucose

redoxReaction.definition: A chemical reaction where electrons are transferred between substances, resulting in a change in their oxidation states, such as photosynthesis and cellular respiration

aerobicRespiration.definition: The cellular process in which organisms use oxygen to convert nutrients, primarily glucose, into chemical energy in the form of ATP

matrix.definition: The innermost compartment of a mitochondrion, containing enzymes and other molecules necessary for cellular respiration, such as those for the citric acid cycle

intermembraneSpace.definition: The compartment of a mitochondrion or chloroplast located between its outer and inner membranes, where oxidative phosphorylation and chemiosmosis take place

cellularRespiration.definition: The process where cells break down biological fuels, like glucose, in the presence of an electron acceptor (usually oxygen) to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP)

glycolysis.definition: The initial, ancient metabolic process in which a molecule of glucose is broken down into two molecules of pyruvate, producing a net gain of  2 ATP and 2 NADH

pyruvate.definition: The natural end-product of glycolysis, a 3 carbon compound which is further broken down in the link reaction and citric acid cycle

nadh.definition: A coenzyme used to donate electrons for oxidative phosphorylation in cellular respiration. NAD+ is the form that accepts electrons, and NADH donates them

linkReaction.definition: Critical intermediate step in cellular respiration that converts the three-carbon pyruvate, a product of glycolysis, into the two-carbon acetyl-CoA

acetylCoA.definition: A critical metabolic molecule that provides acetyl groups for the citric acid cycle

krebsCycle.definition: Central metabolic pathway in the mitochondrial matrix that completes the breakdown of glucose and to generate energy and reduces electron carriers FAD and NAD+ to FADH2 and NADH

fadh2.definition: A coenzyme used to donate electrons for oxidative phosphorylation in cellular respiration. FAD is the form that accepts electrons, and FADH2 donates them

oxidativePhosphorylation.definition: The final stage of aerobic respiration, occurring in the mitochondrial intermembrane space, where the energy released from NADH and FADH2 is used to generate a large amount of ATP

anaerobicRespiration.definition: A metabolic process where cells generate energy (ATP) in the absence of oxygen, primarily through glycolysis

alcoholicFermentation.definition: The anaerobic process where yeast converts glucose and other sugars into ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide through glycolysis, generating ATP

lacticAcidRespiration.definition: The anaerobic process in which glucose or other six-carbon sugars are converted into lactic acid and ATP through glycolysis

signalTransductionPathway.definition: Sequences of biochemical events that translate external signals into internal cell responses, involving ligand-receptor binding, activation of intracellular molecules, and a change in behavior

receptor.definition: A protein that receives specific chemical signals from outside a cell, specific in shape and only able to bind to certain signals, which triggers a cellular response

ligand.definition: A molecule or ion that binds to a central atom or molecule, acting as a signaling molecule that binds to a receptor

autocrineSignaling.definition: Form of cell communication where a cell releases a signal molecule that acts on its own receptors, triggering specific cellular responses

juxtacrineSignaling.definition: A form of direct cell-to-cell communication where surface molecules on one cell bind to receptors on an adjacent cell, requiring direct physical contact for the signal to be transmitted

gapJunction.definition: A protein-lined channel that directly connects the cytoplasm of two adjacent animal cells, allowing for the rapid exchange of ions and small molecules between them

paracrineSignaling.definition: A form of cell-to-cell communication where a cell releases signaling molecules that affect only nearby cells, acting as a local signal

neuroTransmitter.definition: A chemical messenger released by a neuron to transmit a signal to a target cell, such as another neuron, muscle cell, or gland, across a synapse

quorumSensing.definition: A cell-to-cell communication system used by bacteria to monitor population density and coordinate collective behaviors

endocrineSignaling.definition: A form of long-distance cell communication where hormones are secreted by specialized cells into the bloodstream to travel to and act on distant target cells

hormone.definition: Chemical messengers produced by endocrine glands in the body that travel through the bloodstream to target organs and tissues to regulate processes and maintain homeostasis

insulin.definition: A hormone produced by the pancreas that plays a crucial role in regulating blood sugar levels

growthHormone.definition: A protein hormone produced and secreted by the pituitary gland that promotes growth in children, regulates metabolism, and maintains tissues and organs

steroidHormone.definition: Hormones which are steroids, playing a crucial role in sexual development (eg. estrogen), maintaining metabolism, and Vitamin D

cellSurfaceReceptor.definition: Integral proteins in the cell membrane that receive signals from extracellular molecules to trigger a cellular response

ligandGatedIonChannel.definition: Transmembrane proteins that act as channels for ions lto cross the cell membrane, opening their pore in response to a ligand

gProteinCoupledReceptor.definition: Cell surface receptors that activate G proteins when bound to a ligand, triggering downstream cellular cascades

gProtein.definition: Proteins that act as molecular switches inside cells, and are involved in transmitting signals from a variety of stimuli outside a cell to its interior

receptorTyrosineKinase.definition: Cell surface receptors that mediate cell-to-cell communication and control a wide range of complex biological functions, including cell growth, motility, differentiation, and metabolism

phosphorylationCascade.definition: A series of sequential biochemical reactions where one protein kinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to another protein, activating it, and this process repeats in a chain reaction

kinase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the transfer of a phosphate group from ATP to a specified molecule

phosphatase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the removal of a phosphate group from a molecule in a process called dephosphorylation

secondMessenger.definition: Small molecules or ions inside cells that amplify and relay signals from cell-surface receptors to trigger intracellular responses, such as cell growth, muscle contraction, and gene transcription

calciumIon.definition: A calcium atom that has lost two electrons; a very commonly used second messenger

cyclicAMP.definition: A second messenger, or cellular signal occurring within cells, that is important in many biological processes, often transferring a signal to a phosphorylation cascade

geneExpression.definition: The process by which cells use DNA's instructions to create a functional product, typically a protein, through two main steps: transcription and translation

transcriptionFactor.definition: Proteins that regulate gene expression by binding to specific DNA sequences and either activating or repressing transcription

metabolicResponse.definition: An organism’s collection of reactions to a specific signal which results in changes to maintain homeostasis or adapt to the new state

apoptosis.definition: The process of programmed cell death, a controlled and orderly process vital for development, homeostasis, and eliminating damaged cells

epinephrine.definition: A hormone and neurotransmitter from the adrenal glands that triggers the body's "fight-or-flight" response to stress, increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and airflow to the lungs

environmentalFactor.definition: External influences on an organism's growth and development, which can be biotic (living) or abiotic (non-living)

mutation.definition: A permanent change in the DNA sequence of an organism, which can result from copying errors during cell division or damage from environmental factors like radiation and chemicals

inhibitor.definition: A molecule that slows or blocks the activity of another biological molecule, most commonly an enzyme, by binding to it and altering its structure or function

activator.definition: A molecule that increases the activity of another biological molecule, most commonly an enzyme, by binding to it and altering its structure or function

homeostasis.definition: The biological process of maintaining a stable, constant internal environment within an organism despite changes in the external environment

negativeFeedback.definition: A process where the output of a system is fed back to counteract or reduce changes, helping to maintain stability

glucagon.definition: A hormone produced by the pancreas that plays a crucial role in regulating blood sugar levels, stimulating the liver to release stored sugar into the bloodstream

diabetes.definition: A chronic condition that affects how the body uses glucose for energy, due to a body not being able to produce enough insulin or use insulin

positiveFeedback.definition: A process where a stimulus triggers a response that amplifies the original stimulus, causing the system to move further from its initial state

cellCycle.definition: The life cycle of a cell, a series of growth, DNA replication, and division steps that result in two genetically identical daughter cells, divided into 2 phases of interphase and mitosis

interphase.definition: The longest phase of the cell cycle, during which a cell grows, duplicates its DNA, and prepares for cell division

g1Phase.definition: The first stage of interphase in the cell cycle, where the cell grows physically, makes new proteins and organelles, and monitors its environment, preparing for DNA replication

sPhase.definition: The part of the cell cycle following G1 where DNA is replicated, where each chromosome is copied to form two identical sister chromatids

genome.definition: An organism's complete set of DNA, which contains all the information needed for development, function, and reproduction

dnaReplication.definition: The process of making a complete copy of a cell's DNA before it divides through various enzymes, ensuring each daughter cell receives an identical set of genetic instructions

sisterChromatid.definition: Two identical copies of a single chromosome, formed after DNA replication and joined together by a centromere

g2Phase.definition: The third and final stage of interphase in the cell cycle, occurring after S phase, during which the cell grows, synthesizes proteins and organelles, and confirms it is ready for division

g0.definition: Stage of the cell cycle where cells are not dividing or preparing to divide, which cells enter from G1 and in which cells remain permanently or unless they receive signals to re-enter the cycle

mitosis.definition: The process of cell division where one cell divides into two genetically identical daughter cells

prophase.definition: The first stage of cell division, during which condenses chromatin into visible chromosomes, forms the mitotic spindle, and breaks down the nuclear envelope and nucleolus

metaphase.definition: The stage in cell division where chromosomes, fully condensed, line up along the cell's equator on the metaphase plate

anaphase.definition: The stage of cell division where sister chromatids separate and move to opposite ends of the cell

telophase.definition: The final phase of cell division, in which the separated sister chromatids at opposite ends of the cell recondense and form two nuclei, resulting in two daughter cells

cytokinesis.definition: The process following telophase where a cell's cytoplasm splits to form two genetically identical daughter cells

cleavageFurrow.definition: An indentation in the surface of a dividing animal cell that forms during cytokinesis to split the cytoplasm into two separate daughter cells

cellPlate.definition: A structure that forms during the division of plant cells to create a new cell wall, separating the two daughter cells

binaryFission.definition: An asexual reproduction process in which a single-celled organism divides into two identical daughter cells

somaticCell.definition: Any cell of a living organism other than the reproductive cells

diploidCell.definition: Contains two complete sets of chromosomes, one inherited from each parent (46 chromosomes in humans)

gamete.definition: A mature haploid cell which is able to unite with another of the opposite sex in sexual reproduction to form a zygote

haploidCell.definition: Contains one complete set of chromosomes, representing half the genetic material of a typical eukaryotic cell (23 chromosomes in humans)

cellCycleCheckpoint.definition: Crucial regulatory mechanisms that monitor the cell division process, ensuring that DNA is replicated correctly and chromosomes are accurately segregated before the cell divides

cyclinDependentKinase.definition: Enzymes that regulate key cellular processes like the cell cycle by adding phosphate groups to other proteins

growthFactor.definition: Proteins that promote cell growth, differentiation, division, and survival

densityDependentInhibition.definition: A cellular process where cells stop dividing when they become too crowded, which prevents uncontrolled growth in a single layer, and which cancer cells ignore

anchorageDependency.definition: The biological requirement for cells to be attached to a substrate or surface to survive, grow, and divide, preventing uncontrollable cellular growth, which cancer cells ignore

cancer.definition: A group of diseases characterized by the uncontrolled growth and spread of abnormal cells, which can form tumors and invade other tissues

tumor.definition: An abnormal mass of tissue that forms when cells grow and divide uncontrollably

benignTumor.definition: A non-cancerous growth that does not spread to other parts of the body

malignantTumor.definition: A cancerous growth of cells that can invade surrounding tissues and spread to distant parts of the body

metastisis.definition: The process by which cancer cells spread from their original (primary) tumor to other parts of the body

gene.definition: Segments of DNA that carry the instructions for building proteins or functional RNA molecules, acting as the fundamental units of heredity

asexualReproduction.definition: A biological process where a single parent organism creates one or more genetically identical offspring, known as clones

sexualReproduction.definition: A biological process that produces new, genetically unique offspring by combining genetic material from two parents

homologousChromosome.definition: Pairs of chromosomes within a diploid cell that share the same size, shape, and gene locations, but may carry different versions (alleles) of those genes

autosome.definition: Any chromosome that is not a sex chromosome

sexChromosome.definition: A type of chromosome involved in determining an individual's sex; in humans X or Y

meiosis.definition: A type of cell division in sexually reproducing organisms that produces gametes with half the number of chromosomes as the parent cell, resulting in genetically unique, haploid cells

fertilization.definition: The biological process where a male gamete (sperm) and a female gamete (egg) fuse to form a single cell called a zygote, initiating the development of a new individual

synapsis.definition: The fusion of chromosome pairs at the start of meiosis

crossingOver.definition: A biological process in meiosis where homologous chromosomes exchange genetic material, creating recombinant chromosomes with a mix of genes from both parents

independentAssortment.definition: The randomness and separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis 1, increasing genetic variation

randomFertilization.definition: The principle that any given sperm can fertilize any given egg, resulting in an enormous number of unique genetic combinations in sexually reproducing organisms

genotype.definition: An organism's specific set of genetic information or the variant forms (alleles) of a particular gene that it carries

phenotype.definition: The set of observable characteristics or traits of an organism

dominantAllele.definition: A version of a gene that expresses its trait in an individual's phenotype even when only one copy of the allele is present (denoted by a capital letter)

recessiveAllele.definition: A version of a gene that expresses its trait in an individual's phenotype only when both copies of the allele are present, and the individual has no dominant alleles (denoted by a lowercase letter)

homozygous.definition: Having inherited the same alleles of a genomic marker from each biological parent, meaning two identical copies of the allele within the individual

heterozygous.definition: Having inherited different alleles of a genomic marker from each biological parent, meaning each allele within the individual will be different

punnettSquare.definition: A genetics tool that uses a simple grid to predict the potential genotypes (alleles) and phenotypes (observable traits) of offspring from a genetic cross

lawOfSegregation.definition: Principle of Mendelian genetics stating that the two alleles of an individual for a given gene separate during the formation of gametes, ensuring that each gamete receives only one allele

testCross.definition: A genetic experiment to determine if an individual with a dominant phenotype has a homozygous dominant or heterozygous genotype by crossing it with a recessive individual

monohybridCross.definition: A genetics cross between two individuals that differ in only one trait

lawOfIndependentAssortment.definition: Principle of Mendelian genetics stating that alleles for different genes segregate independently of one another during gamete formation

dihybridCross.definition: A genetic cross between two individuals that differ in two traits, resulting in a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation when crossing heterozygous individuals

chiSquareTest.definition: A statistical method for determining if there is a significant difference between an observed frequency distribution and an expected one

nullHypothesis.definition: A statement that there is no significant effect, relationship, or difference between variables in a population; the default assumption within an experiment

completeDominance.definition: A form of Mendelian inheritance where one allele (the dominant allele) completely masks the effect of another allele (the recessive allele) for a specific trait

incompleteDominance.definition: A genetic inheritance pattern where neither of two alleles is completely dominant or recessive, resulting in a blended or intermediate phenotype in the heterozygous individual

codominance.definition: A genetic inheritance pattern where both alleles for a trait are fully and simultaneously expressed in the phenotype of a heterozygous individual

multipleAllele.definition: Three or more different versions of the same gene found within a population

linkedGene.definition: Genes located on the same chromosome that tend to be inherited together due to their physical proximity, and do not independently assort

linageMap.definition: A diagram showing the relative positions and genetic distances between genes on a chromosome, based on the frequency of recombination (crossing over) during meiosis

parentalType.definition: Offspring whose allele combinations for specific genes are identical to the allele combinations of one of their parents

recombinantType.definition: Offspring whose allele combinations for specific genes are not identical to the allele combinations of one of their parents

nonnuclearInheritance.definition: The inheritance of genes from structures other than the nucleus, such as the mitochondria

sexLinkedGene.definition: A gene located on one of the sex chromosomes, either the X or Y chromosome, which have unique patterns of inheritance due to the combinations of these chromosomes in different sexes

pedigree.definition: A diagram of a family tree that uses standardized symbols to show relationships and the inheritance of traits or genetic diseases across generations

polygenicInheritance.definition: A type of genetic inheritance where a single trait is influenced by multiple genes, rather than just one gene

phenotypicPlasticity.definition: The ability of a single genotype to produce different phenotypes (observable characteristics) in response to different environmental conditions, such as temperature, diet, or predators

purine.definition: A category of nitrogenous bases containing two carbon rings, such as adenine and guanine

pyrimidine.definition: A category of nitrogenous bases containing one carbon ring, such as thymine, cytosine, and uracil

histoneProtein.definition: Basic proteins found in the nuclei of eukaryotic cells that organize and compact DNA into chromosomes

nucleosome.definition: The basic unit of DNA packaging in eukaryotes, consisting of a segment of DNA wrapped around a spool of eight histone proteins

chromatin.definition: The complex of DNA and proteins (primarily histones) that forms chromosomes in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, which condenses to form chromosomes during cell division

intron.definition: Non-coding sequences of DNA found within a gene that are transcribed into RNA but are removed before the RNA is translated into a protein

exon.definition: Coding sequences of DNA that are transcribed into RNA and are translated into a protein

linearChromosome.definition: Rod-shaped structures found in eukaryotic cell nuclei that contain genetic information, which contain telomeres on their ends and a central centromere

circularChromosome.definition: A ring-shaped molecule of DNA, found primarily in prokaryotes and certain organelles (like mitochondria and chloroplasts)

plasmid.definition: Small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules that are separate from a cell's main chromosome and can replicate independently

semiconservativeProcess.definition: A method of DNA replication where each new DNA molecule consists of one original ("parental") strand and one newly synthesized strand

helicase.definition: An enzyme that unwinds double-stranded DNA and RNA by breaking the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, creating a replication fork

topoisomerase.definition: Enzyme that manages DNA topology by cutting and resealing DNA strands to relieve the tension from supercoiling which occurs as helicase unwinds the DNA

dnaPolymerase.definition: A crucial enzyme that synthesizes DNA by adding nucleotides to a growing strand, adding complementary nitrogenous bases in a 5’ to 3’ direction

leadingStrand.definition: The new DNA strand synthesized continuously in the 5’ to 3’ direction, moving along with the replication fork

laggingStrand.definition: The new DNA strand synthesized discontinuously in the 3’ to 5’ direction in fragments because its template runs against the replication fork

okazakiFragment.definition: Short DNA sequences that are synthesized discontinuously on the lagging strand during DNA replication

ligase.definition: An enzyme that catalyzes the formation of phosphodiester bonds, such as those which connect Okazaki fragments to create a continuous strand of DNA

telomere.definition: Protective caps at the ends of chromosomes that consist of repetitive DNA sequences and proteins

centralDogma.definition: Describes the flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein, through the processes of transcription (DNA to RNA) and translation (RNA to protein)

transcription.definition: The biological process of creating an mRNA copy from a DNA template using RNA polymerase

mRNA.definition: A single-stranded RNA molecule that carries genetic instructions from DNA to the cell's ribosomes for protein synthesis

templateStrand.definition: A single strand of DNA that serves as a pattern for synthesizing a complementary strand of RNA during transcription or a new DNA strand during replication

codingStrand.definition: The DNA strand with the same sequence as the mRNA that is transcribed from it, with the exception of having thymine instead of uracil

rnaPolymerase.definition: A crucial enzyme that transcribes DNA into RNA by binding to a DNA promoter sequence and synthesizing a complementary RNA strand

5cap.definition: A modification at the 5' end of mRNA where a guanine nucleotide is added to the beginning of the transcript, protecting it from degradation and helping ribosomes bind to it

polyATail.definition: A modification at the 3' end of mRNA where a string of adenosine nucleotides is added to the end of the transcript, protecting it from degradation and enhancing translation

rnaSplicing.definition: The process of removing non-coding regions called introns from the precursor pre-mRNA and joining the coding regions called exons to form mRNA

spliceosome.definition: A molecular machine made of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) and proteins that removes introns from pre-mRNA and joins the exons together to create mature mRNA

ribozyme.definition: A catalytic RNA molecule that functions like an enzyme, assisting in protein synthesis and mRNA processing

translation.definition: The process of creating a protein from an mRNA template, which involves reading the genetic code on the mRNA in three-nucleotide units called codons

tRNA.definition: A small RNA molecule that functions as an adaptor in protein synthesis, linking the codons on mRNA to the correct amino acids

rRNA.definition: A type of non-coding RNA that is a major structural and functional component of ribosomes, helping bind to mRNA and tRNA and catalyze formation of peptide bonds during translation

codon.definition: A sequence of three nucleotides in a DNA or RNA molecule that specifies a particular amino acid or a start/stop signal for protein synthesis

anticodon.definition: A three-nucleotide sequence on a transfer RNA (tRNA) molecule that is complementary to a three-nucleotide codon on a messenger RNA (mRNA) molecule

signalPeptide.definition: A short amino acid sequence located at the end of a protein that directs its secretion or insertion into a cell membrane

retrovirus.definition: An RNA virus that reverses the typical cellular process of transcription, converting its RNA into DNA after infecting a host cell

reverseTranscriptase.definition: An enzyme that synthesizes DNA from an RNA template, which in the case of retroviruses can then integrate into the host’s DNA and undergo protein synthesis

epigenetics.definition: The study of how behaviors and environment can cause changes that affect the way genes work without altering the underlying DNA sequence

dnaMethylation.definition: An epigenetic process that adds a methyl group to DNA, which can turn genes "off" and silence their activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence by tightening the DNA

histoneAcetylation.definition: An epigenetic process where an acetyl group is added to histone proteins, making the DNA more accessible to transcription machinery and enhancing expression by loosening the DNA

regulatorySequence.definition: Segments of DNA that control gene expression by binding to proteins and influencing processes like transcription and translation, such as promoters, enhancers, and silencers

constitutiveGene.definition: Genes that are continuously expressed at a relatively constant level, providing proteins needed for basic cellular functions and maintenance

inducibleExpression.definition: A method of gene regulation where a gene's activity is turned on or off by the presence of a specific inducer molecule

transcriptionInitiationComplex.definition: A group of proteins that assembles at a gene's promoter region to begin transcription, as well as regulatory sequences and transcription factors

enhancer.definition: A DNA region that can increase the rate of gene transcription by binding proteins called transcription factors

promoter.definition: A DNA sequence located upstream of a gene that acts as the binding site for RNA polymerase and transcription factors, initiating the process of transcription

alternativeRNASplicing.definition: A process where introns are removed from pre-mRNA and exons are joined together in different combinations, creating multiple mature mRNA transcripts from a single gene

ubiquitin.definition: A protein found in most eukaryotic cells that acts as a tag to regulate the function of other proteins, such as making the protein a target for degradation or changing its function

inducibleOperon.definition: A gene cluster regulated by an "inducer" molecule that turns on transcription, allowing the cell to produce enzymes to break down a specific substrate, innately “off” when the substrate is absent

repressibleOperon.definition: A gene cluster regulated by an "repressor" molecule that turns off transcription, allowing the cell to produce certain molecules, innately “on” when the substrate is absent

operator.definition: A segment of DNA where a repressor protein binds to control gene transcription

repressor.definition: A protein that inhibits gene expression by binding to the operator and blocking transcription

cellDifferentiation.definition: The process by which an unspecialized cell becomes a specialized type of cell through the activation and silencing of specific genes

differentialGeneExpression.definition: The biochemical process that determinates which genes respond to which signals or triggers depending on the conditions

cellSpecialization.definition: The unique structure and function differentiated cells acquire,”what” the cell’s role is

smallRNA.definition: Group of short, non-coding RNA molecules that play vital roles in regulating gene expression

miRNA.definition: A small RNA which regulates gene expression through RNA interference, inhibiting translation

siRNA.definition: A small RNA which regulates gene expression by degrading mRNA

pointMutation.definition: A change in a single nucleotide base pair in the DNA sequence, such as a substitution, insertion, or deletion

insertion.definition: A type of genetic change where one or more nucleotide pairs are inserted into the DNA sequence

deletion.definition: A type of genetic change where one or more nucleotide pairs are removed from the DNA sequence

frameshiftMutation.definition: A type of genetic mutation where one or more nucleotides are inserted or deleted from a DNA sequence, causing the reading frame of the gene to shift, changing the codon groupings

nonsenseMutation.definition: A type of point mutation in which a nucleotide base pair is changed, resulting in a premature stop codon (UAG, UGA, or UAA) in the mRNA transcript

silentMutation.definition: A type of mutation where a nucleotide base pair in the DNA sequence is altered, but this change does not change the produced amino acid sequence due to the redundancy of the genetic code

codonChart.definition: A table which can be used to translate a genetic code into a sequence of amino acids by using mRNA codons

mutagen.definition: An agent, such as radiation or a chemical substance, which causes genetic mutation

nondisjunction.definition: The failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during mitosis or meiosis, resulting in daughter cells with an incorrect number of chromosomes

horizontalGeneTransfer.definition: The transfer of genetic material between organisms that are not parent and offspring through transformation, conjugation, and transduction in bacteria, and through viruses in eukaryotes

transformation.definition: The process where a bacterium takes up external DNA from its environment, which can change its genetic makeup

transduction.definition: The process of transferring genetic material from one bacterium to another via a virus, or bacteriophage

conjugation.definition: A process of horizontal gene transfer where genetic material, typically a plasmid, is transferred directly from one bacterium to another through a connection

transposition.definition: A process in which genetic elements, called transposons, move from one location to another within the genome of a bacterium

virus.definition: A submicroscopic infectious agent that replicates only inside the living cells of an organism

biotechnology.definition: The use of living organisms, cells, and biological processes to develop products and technologies for a wide range of applications, including medicine, agriculture, and industry

dnaSequencing.definition: The process of determining the order of the four nucleotide bases (A, C, G, and T) in a DNA molecule, which provides the instructions for an organism's cells

gelElectrophoresis.definition: A laboratory technique that separates DNA, RNA, or proteins based on their size and electrical charge, allowing analysis and comparison of DNA samples

pcr.definition: A laboratory technique used to rapidly amplify a specific segment of DNA through the use of RNA polymerase, creating millions of copies from a small sample

recombinantDNA.definition: DNA from different sources that has been combined in a laboratory setting, often through the use of a plasmid

geneCloning.definition: The process of making identical copies of a specific gene or DNA segment by introducing the specific DNA segment into a fast reproducing host organism, such as bacteria

restrictionEnzyme.definition: Proteins that cut DNA at specific sequences, acting as "molecular scissors" for a variety of biotechnology applications

crisprCas9.definition: A genome-editing technology that uses a guide RNA to direct the Cas9 protein, which acts like molecular scissors, to cut DNA at a specific location

evolution.definition: The process of cumulative changes in the inherited traits of a population over generations, leading to the development of new species, driven by both natural selection and random events

charlesDarwin.definition: An English naturalist and biologist who proposed that all species of life have descended from a common ancestor and the theory of natural selection

adaptation.definition: A heritable trait—a physical structure, physiological process, or behavior—that increases an organism's ability to survive and reproduce in its environment

naturalSelection.definition: The process by which organisms with traits better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully, causing those traits to become more common over generations

biologicalFitness.definition: An organism's ability to survive and produce offspring with heritable traits that are passed to future generations (ie. reproductive success)

population.definition: A group of individuals of the same species living in the same geographic area at the same time

ddtResistance.definition: A random genetic mutation in insects which allowed these individuals to survive DDT and reproduce, increasing the frequency of the resistance gene in the population over time

sickleCellAnemia.definition: An inherited disorder characterized which causes red blood cells to take on a crescent moon shape, leading to blockages of small blood vessels

heterozygoteAdvantage.definition: A genetic phenomenon where a heterozygote has a higher relative fitness than either of the two homozygote

artificialSelection.definition: The process where humans deliberately breed organisms with desirable traits to produce offspring with those same traits

alleleFrequency.definition: The measure of how common a specific allele is within a population, calculated by dividing the number of copies of that allele by the total number of copies of all alleles for that gene

disruptiveSelection.definition: A type of selection where extreme traits are favored over intermediate ones, increasing variation within a population and resulting in a population with two or more distinct phenotypes

stabilizingSelection.definition: A type of selection that favors intermediate phenotypes and acts against extreme variations, leading to a stable population with reduced genetic diversity

directionalSelection.definition: A type of selection where one extreme phenotype is favored over others, causing a shift in the population's average trait over time

balancingSelection.definition: A type of selection that maintains genetic diversity within a population by favoring multiple alleles over time, rather than allowing one allele to become dominant

frequencyDependentSelection.definition: A driver of balancing selection where the fitness of a trait depends on its frequency within a population meaning either common traits have higher fitness or rarer traits have higher fitness

geneticDrift.definition: The change in the frequency of an existing gene variant in a population due to random chance, rather than natural selection

founderEffect.definition: A type of genetic drift that occurs when a new population is established by a small number of individuals from a larger population, leading to reduced genetic diversity

bottleneckEffect.definition: A sharp reduction in a population's genetic diversity caused by a catastrophic event, such as a natural disaster or human activity, which drastically decreases the number of individuals

geneFlow.definition: The movement of genes between populations, which happens when individuals or their genetic material migrate and successfully reproduce

sexualSelection.definition: An evolutionary process driven by competition for mates and resulting in reproductive success

sexualDimorphism.definition: The difference in appearance between males and females of the same species, including variations in size, color, or structure, leading to adaptations that are important for reproduction

hardyWeinbergEquilibrium.definition: A principle that states a population's allele and genotype frequencies will remain constant from generation to generation if no evolutionary forces are acting upon it

antibioticResistance.definition: Occurs when bacteria evolve to resist medicines meant to kill them through mutations, acquiring resistance genes, and developing antibiotic countering enzymes

homology.definition: Biological features including genes and their products that are descended from a feature present in a common ancestor

homologousStructure.definition: Body parts in different species that have a similar underlying anatomy and origin from a common ancestor, but serve different functions

embryonicHomology.definition: Structural similarities in the embryos of different species that reveal their shared ancestry

molecularHomology.definition: Similarities in DNA, RNA, or protein sequences between different species, indicating a shared evolutionary origin

vestigialOrgan.definition: Evolutionary remnants, body parts or behaviors in an organism that have lost most or all of their original function from an ancestor but still exist, serving as evidence for common ancestry

convergentEvolution.definition: When distantly related organisms independently evolve similar traits or features because they adapt to similar environments, not because they share a recent common ancestor

analogousStructure.definition: Body parts in different species that have similar functions but evolved independently

fossil.definition: Preserved remains, impressions, or traces of ancient living things from past geological ages

fossilRecord.definition: The collection of all discovered fossils, showing changes in organisms over time and acting as evidence for evolutio

biogeography.definition: The scientific study of how life (species and ecosystems) is distributed across Earth in space and time

continentalDrift.definition: The theory that the Earth's continents were once joined as a single supercontinent called Pangaea and have since slowly moved apart to their current positions

endemicSpecies.definition: A plant or animal found naturally in only one specific geographic location, leading to the formation of specialized adaptations for that environment

phylogeny.definition: The representation of the evolutionary history and relationships between groups of organisms based on their observable characteristics

phylogeneticTree.definition: A branching diagram that visually represents the evolutionary relationships and shared ancestry among different species or groups, often showing evolutionary time and genetic distance

taxon.definition: Any named, hierarchical group of organisms classified together in biology based on shared ancestry and characteristics

branchPoint.definition: Mark an evolutionary divergence, showing where one ancestral lineage split into two or more distinct new ones, representing a common ancestor for all groups that branch off from that spot

outgroup.definition: A closely related organism outside the main group of interest used as a reference to root a phylogenetic tree, clarifying which features are ancestral and which are unique to the ingroup

sisterTaxa.definition: Two groups on a phylogenetic tree that are each other's closest evolutionary relatives, diverging from the same ancestral node more recently than any other groups on the tree

molecularClock.definition: A method using DNA or protein mutation rates to estimate evolutionary timelines, with more genetic differences indicating a longer time since species diverged from a common ancestor

cladogram.definition: Diagrams which depict the relationships between different groups of taxa called “clades,” showing only the order of evolutionary divergence based on shared traits

clade.definition: A group of organisms consisting of a common ancestor and all of its descendants

sharedDerivedCharacteristic.definition: Unique traits inherited from a recent common ancestor that define a specific group (clade) and distinguish it from more distant relatives, used to construct evolutionary trees

sharedAncestralCharacteristic.definition: Characteristics present in a common ancestor of a group and inherited by all its descendants

species.definition: A unit in biological classification, representing the largest group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring, characterized by common traits and shared genes

speciation.definition: The evolutionary process where one species splits into two or more new, distinct species, driven by reproductive isolation and genetic divergence

reproductiveIsolation.definition: Biological barriers that stop different species from breeding and producing fertile offspring, ultimately leading to speciation

prezygoticBarrier.definition: Biological mechanisms that prevent different species from mating or successfully fertilizing eggs. Types include temporal, behavioral, mechanical, habitat, and gametic isolation.

postzygoticBarrier.definition: Biological mechanisms that prevent hybrid zygotes from developing into fertile adults. Types include reduced hybrid viability, reduced hybrid fertility, and hybrid breakdown.

allopatricSpeciation.definition: The evolution of new species from a single ancestral species due to geographic isolation, where physical barriers split a population and prevent gene flow, resulting in reproductive isolation

sympatricSpeciation.definition: The evolution of new species from a single ancestral group while both continue to live in the same geographic area, driven by behavioral isolation and chromosomal changes

polyploidy.definition: A condition where cells have more than two complete sets of chromosomes, causing instant reproductive isolation from the parent species and leading to new species formation

hybridZone.definition: A geographic area where two distinct but related populations or species meet, interbreed, and produce hybrid offspring

divergentEvolution.definition: When closely related populations from a common ancestor evolve different traits, often due to adapting to different environments or ecological niches, leading to new species

adaptiveRadiation.definition: The rapid diversification of a single ancestral species into many new species, each adapted to a unique ecological niche

punctuatedEquilibrium.definition: An evolutionary theory proposing that species experience long periods of little to no change interrupted by short bursts of significant evolutionary change that lead to speciation

gradualism.definition: The theory that major evolutionary changes result from the slow, steady accumulation of small, incremental variations over vast periods, contrasting with sudden bursts of change

geneticVariation.definition: Differences in DNA among individuals, which is crucial for natural selection and evolution to take place

selectivePressure.definition: Environmental or biological factors (like predators, food scarcity, climate, or mates) that influence which organisms in a population survive and reproduce
